conventional_description: Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a slow-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow, caused by a genetic mutation known as the Philadelphia chromosome. This mutation leads to the overproduction of abnormal white blood cells. The disease typically progresses through three phases - chronic, accelerated, and blast crisis. Common symptoms include fatigue, unintended weight loss, night sweats, and a feeling of fullness or discomfort in the left upper abdomen from an enlarged spleen. Diagnosis is confirmed through blood tests and a bone marrow biopsy, and monitoring involves regular blood counts and PCR testing for the BCR-ABL gene.
conventional_treatments: The cornerstone of treatment is a class of drugs called tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as imatinib, which target the abnormal protein produced by the Philadelphia chromosome. These medications can achieve long-term remission in many patients. Other options include chemotherapy, interferon, and in selected cases, allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Regular monitoring is essential to assess response and detect any signs of resistance or progression.
tcm_understanding:
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is understood as a deep disorder of the marrow, which is governed by the Kidneys. The Kidneys store essence (Jing) and produce marrow - the very substance that generates healthy blood. When this essence is depleted by constitutional weakness, overwork, or chronic illness, the marrow fails to produce adequate Qi and Blood, leading to the profound fatigue, pallor, and weakness that mark the early chronic phase.
The Spleen also plays a critical role, because it transforms food into the Qi and Blood that nourish the whole body. When the Spleen is weakened, the source of new blood is cut off, compounding the deficiency. Over time, Qi deficiency slows the movement of Blood, creating stagnation. This is why many people with CML develop an enlarged spleen - in TCM, a fixed abdominal mass is a classic sign of Blood stasis, often with underlying Qi deficiency.
As the disease persists, the deeper reserves of Kidney Yin and Yang begin to fail. Kidney Yin deficiency brings night sweats, low-grade fevers, and a dry, hot sensation in the palms and soles. Kidney Yang deficiency leads to a deep, unremitting coldness, especially in the lower back and knees.
In advanced or blast crisis stages, the long-standing deficiency can suddenly give way to an explosive accumulation of Toxic-Heat, causing high fever, severe bleeding, and overwhelming infection. This is why TCM sees CML not as one uniform disease, but as a spectrum of patterns - from pure deficiency to stagnation to life-threatening heat - each requiring a fundamentally different treatment approach.
classical_quote: 「精脱者，耳聋；气脱者，目不明；津脱者，腠理开，汗大泄；液脱者，骨属屈伸不利，色夭，脑髓消，胫酸，耳数鸣；血脱者，色白，夭然不泽，其脉空虚，此其候也。」
classical_translation: "When essence is depleted, there is deafness; when Qi is depleted, the eyes lose clarity; when fluids are depleted, the pores open and there is profuse sweating; when humors are depleted, the joints become stiff, the complexion withers, the brain marrow diminishes, the shins ache, and the ears ring frequently; when blood is depleted, the complexion is white and lusterless, and the pulse is empty - these are the signs."
classical_source:
Huangdi Neijing, Suwen  ,  Chapter 23, On Depletion of Essence, Qi, Fluids, Humors, and Blood 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
To understand which pattern is at play, a TCM practitioner first asks about your energy, your complexion, and any sense of fullness or discomfort in the left upper abdomen. Fatigue and pallor that appear early, without much abdominal distension, lean strongly toward a simple deficiency of Qi and Blood. A heavy, dragging sensation under the ribs shifts the picture toward Blood Stagnation, even when the other signs are mild.
If you also notice night sweats, a low‑grade fever that comes and goes, or a dry throat that bothers you more in the evening, the practitioner looks for signs of Kidney Yin Deficiency. The tongue may appear red with a thin or absent coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid - clues that the body’s cooling, nourishing Yin is being consumed.
When the story changes to feeling chronically cold, with a deep weariness that rest does not fix, the focus moves to Kidney Yang Deficiency. Here the tongue is often pale and puffy, and the pulse feels deep and slow. Some people show a mix of both: alternating waves of heat and cold, or a tongue that looks partly red and partly pale, which suggests both Yin and Yang are depleted together.
A sudden shift is the most important alarm. High fever, unexpected bleeding, or severe infections signal an eruption of Toxic‑Heat, usually during a blast crisis or acute transformation. In this rare but dangerous pattern, the tongue becomes red with a thick yellow coat and the pulse is rapid and forceful. This picture requires urgent attention and is never treated at home.

patterns.symptoms: ["Persistent, crushing fatigue", "Pale or sallow complexion and lips", "Dizziness and lightheadedness", "Heart palpitations", "Shortness of breath on mild exertion", "Poor appetite and loose stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork or physical strain, Chronic stress and worry, Skipping meals or poor diet, Excessive sweating or blood loss, Raw, cold foods and iced drinks
patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Warm, nourishing cooked meals, Bone broths and soups, Gentle exercise or movement
patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the bone marrow's normal blood-forming function is disrupted by the disease. This directly impairs the body's ability to produce healthy Qi and Blood, which are the fundamental substances that nourish every tissue. The Spleen, responsible for transforming food into Qi and Blood, becomes overwhelmed and weak, leading to a state of profound depletion. The result is the hallmark anemia, fatigue, and pallor seen in the chronic phase of CML.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, especially weak at the right middle position (Spleen).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen is the engine of Qi and Blood production, and it thrives on warmth, rest, and easily digested food. Overwork, stress, and poor diet further weaken a Spleen that is already struggling to keep up with the demands of the disease. Conversely, rest and nourishing, warm foods directly feed the Spleen's function, allowing it to slowly rebuild the body's depleted Qi and Blood reserves. This is the foundation for any recovery of strength and vitality.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on easily digestible, nutrient-dense foods like bone broths, congees, and well-cooked root vegetables. Small, frequent meals are better than large ones. Avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle activities like walking or Qigong can help Qi circulate without depleting it; prioritize rest and sleep to allow the body to rebuild.

patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the overproduction of abnormal cells leads to splenomegaly, which in TCM is seen as a mass caused by Qi and Blood stagnation. The prolonged disease weakens Qi, and the sluggish flow of Qi fails to move Blood, causing it to accumulate in the left upper abdomen. This stasis produces a fixed, stabbing pain that worsens with pressure and at night, along with dark lips, nails, and complexion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins. Pulse: choppy (Se) or wiry (Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold causes blood to congeal and stagnate further, while warmth and movement encourage blood to flow. Emotional stress leads to Liver Qi stagnation, which is a major cause of blood stasis; calming the mind and moving the body help unblock Qi. Prolonged sitting impairs circulation in the abdomen, worsening the mass and pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, black pepper, and moderate amounts of red meat. Avoid cold, raw foods and excessive dairy that can congeal blood. Engage in gentle daily exercise like walking or tai chi to promote circulation, and manage stress through meditation to prevent Qi stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Night sweats", "Heat in the palms, soles, and chest (five-centre heat)", "Tidal fever or afternoon low-grade fever", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night", "Dizziness and tinnitus", "Lower back and knee soreness", "Reddish cheeks (malar flush)", "Insomnia with vivid dreams"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and late nights, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Emotional stress or anger, Hot weather or sauna, Excessive sexual activity
patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Cool, quiet environment, Yin-nourishing foods (pears, black sesame), Gentle exercise or movement, Acupuncture and herbal therapy
patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the malignant proliferation of cells gradually exhausts the body's Yin essence, especially that of the Kidney. The Kidney stores essence and governs bone marrow; when its Yin is depleted, the marrow fails to produce healthy blood, leading to anemia and fatigue. The deficiency of Yin allows empty heat to arise, causing night sweats, low-grade fever, and the characteristic five-centre heat. This pattern reflects a deep consumption of the body's foundational Yin, which is common as CML progresses over time.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry, with little or no coating; cracks may be present. Pulse: fine (xi) and rapid (shu), especially weak at the left rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin Deficiency is a state of depleted cooling and moistening resources. Overwork and late nights further drain Yin, while spicy and hot foods add heat that aggravates the empty fire. Emotional stress can also consume Yin and generate internal heat. Rest, especially at night, allows the body to restore Yin. Cooling foods and a calm environment help soothe the deficiency heat, while gentle movement supports circulation without depleting fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, yin-nourishing foods like pears, black sesame seeds, goji berries, and bone broths. Avoid spicy, fried, and overly warming foods that consume yin. Prioritize sleep and avoid staying up late, as the night is when yin is restored. Gentle activities like tai chi or walking are better than intense exercise that depletes fluids.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys store essence and govern bone marrow. When Kidney Yang is deficient, the life-gate fire is too weak to warm the body and transform essence into marrow and blood. This slows blood production, causing fatigue, pallor, and a deep sense of cold. The lack of warmth also leads to cold extremities, lassitude, and a deep slow pulse.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), slow (迟 chí), and weak, especially at the rear positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire. Cold depletes it further, while warmth and rest help preserve it. Raw foods require extra digestive fire to process, straining the already weak Yang. Moxibustion directly adds warmth to the channels and points, rekindling the life-gate fire.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, cooked foods like lamb stew, bone broth, ginger, and walnuts. Avoid raw, cold, and icy foods. Keep the lower back and abdomen warm; use a heating pad or moxibustion on the lower back and below the navel. Gentle daily movement like walking or Tai Chi helps circulate Yang without exhausting it. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, especially in cold weather.

patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the marrow’s ability to produce healthy blood cells depends on the Kidney essence. When the disease persists, both the cooling, moistening Yin and the warming, activating Yang of the Kidneys become exhausted. This leaves the bone marrow without the deep reserves it needs, so Qi and Blood are not generated, causing severe fatigue, pallor, and alternating heat and cold signs.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy-tender body with teeth marks and cracks, thin white coat that may be partially peeled. Pulse: deep, fine, and weak, weakest at the Chi position; may be slightly rapid if Yin deficiency dominates or slow if Yang deficiency dominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overwork and exhaustion directly deplete Kidney essence, while cold damages Yang and heat consumes Yin, so a balanced, moderate environment protects both. Spicy, greasy foods create internal damp-heat that further drains Yin and burdens the Spleen. Rest and nourishing foods rebuild the deep reserves of Qi and Blood, and gentle movement circulates without overtaxing the weakened Kidneys.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easy-to-digest foods like congee, bone broths, and stews with root vegetables. Avoid icy drinks and raw foods that chill the interior, as well as spicy, greasy items that overheat and consume Yin. Gentle daily movement such as tai chi or walking helps circulate Qi without draining reserves. Prioritize rest and sleep to allow the Kidneys to recharge.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure chronic myelogenous leukemia?
faqs.answer: TCM is not a standalone cure for CML, and it should never replace conventional TKI therapy. However, it can play a valuable supportive role. By strengthening Qi and Blood, nourishing Kidney essence, and clearing stagnation or heat, TCM may help improve energy, reduce symptoms, and enhance your body's resilience. Many patients find that combining TCM with their standard treatment leads to a better quality of life and fewer side effects.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my TKI medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only under the guidance of both your oncologist and a qualified TCM practitioner. Some herbs can influence liver enzyme pathways or have mild effects on blood clotting. Your TCM practitioner will select herbs that are safe and appropriate for your specific pattern and will avoid those known to interact with your medications. Always bring a complete list of your medications to every TCM consultation.

faqs.question: What can acupuncture do for CML?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is used to support the body's organ systems, not to directly treat the cancer. It can help relieve fatigue, reduce pain from an enlarged spleen, ease nausea from medications, and improve sleep. Points like Zusanli (ST-36) and Sanyinjiao (SP-6) are commonly used to strengthen Qi and Blood, while Shenshu (BL-23) and Taixi (KI-3) nourish the Kidneys. Treatment is always gentle and adapted to your current blood counts and energy level.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Many patients notice improved energy, better appetite, and reduced night sweats within the first month of consistent herbal therapy and acupuncture. Changes in blood counts typically take longer - often 2 to 3 months - and require regular monitoring. Deep marrow regeneration is a slow process, and treatment for deficiency patterns may continue for 6 to 12 months or longer. Your TCM practitioner will adjust the formula as your pattern shifts over time.

faqs.question: Are there any dietary changes I should make?
faqs.answer: A warm, nourishing diet is the foundation. Focus on easily digestible cooked foods like soups, congees, and bone broths that support the Spleen and build Blood. Include dark leafy greens, small amounts of high-quality protein, and avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that can weaken digestion. If you have night sweats and a dry mouth, add moistening foods like pear and black sesame. If you feel chronically cold, warming spices like ginger and cinnamon can help. Your practitioner can offer more specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use moxibustion if I have a bleeding tendency?
faqs.answer: Moxibustion - the burning of dried mugwort near acupuncture points - is generally safe when performed by a trained practitioner, but caution is needed if your platelet count is very low. Direct or scarring moxibustion is avoided. Gentle, indirect moxibustion on points like Zusanli (ST-36) or Guanyuan (REN-4) may actually help strengthen the blood and stop bleeding in some deficiency patterns, but it must be carefully evaluated. Always inform your practitioner about your latest blood counts before any treatment.

faqs.question: How does TCM help with the fatigue from CML?
faqs.answer: Fatigue in CML is often a combination of Qi deficiency, Blood deficiency, and Kidney essence depletion. TCM addresses this by using herbs like Huang Qi (Astragalus) and Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis) to boost Qi and nourish Blood, along with acupuncture points that strengthen the Spleen and Kidneys. Unlike stimulants, these treatments aim to rebuild your body's own energy reserves from the ground up. Many patients report a gradual, sustained improvement in stamina and mental clarity.

research.title: Case Examples of Shuyu Wan in Treating Hematological Disorders
research.description: This case series reported on the use of Shuyu Wan in treating various hematological disorders, including chronic myelogenous leukemia. The formula, which tonifies Qi and Blood while mildly resolving stagnation, was associated with improvements in fatigue, anemia, and overall quality of life when used alongside conventional therapy.

research.title: Wang Maosheng's Experience in Treating Chronic Leukemia from the Perspective of Toxin, Stasis, and Deficiency
research.description: This article discusses the clinical experience of treating chronic leukemia, including CML, by addressing the triad of toxin, blood stasis, and deficiency. The author presents cases where a modified Yiqi Huoxue Jiedu Tang formula reduced spleen size, improved blood counts, and alleviated symptoms like fever and bleeding, demonstrating a holistic TCM approach alongside TKI therapy.
